c.statement: An experience is identical to the cause–effect structure (Φ-structure) unfolded from a maximal substrate; this is a fundamental explanatory identity, not a correspondence between two separate things.
The quality and quantity of an experience is completely specified by a maximally irreducible conceptual structure (MICS) and the associated value of integrated information Φ-max.

Consciousness requires intrinsic cause–effect power that is specific, integrated (unitary), definite (exclusive), and structured; substrate must satisfy all five essential phenomenal properties—making it substrate-dependent.
A feed-forward system can be functionally equivalent to a conscious complex yet be unconscious, denying that functional equivalence is sufficient for consciousness.
The quality of experience is accounted for by the way the Φ-structure is composed, which depends on the architecture of the substrate specifying it.
The cerebral cortex can support experience even when almost silent; consciousness does not require active neuronal broadcasting, only intact cause–effect repertoires.
Digital computers with von Neumann architecture are not conscious even when performing complex intelligent functions, because architecture—not computation—determines consciousness.

Integrated information (φ / Φ-structure) is the quantity that determines the presence and level of consciousness; a candidate system must specify a maximum of integrated information to qualify as a substrate.

Global broadcast of neural signals is not necessary for consciousness; conscious content is determined by the shape of the MICS specified by the complex, not by fronto-parietal ignition or global signal propagation.

The quality of experience corresponds to the Φ-structure (set of distinctions and relations), while its quantity (Φ) equals the sum of integrated information values (φd/r) of those distinctions and relations.
The posterior cerebral cortex, organized as a dense divergent-convergent hierarchical lattice of specialized units, is the locus of the substrate of human consciousness.

Integrated information Φ is a quantity measuring the structure integrated information of a complex; higher Φ requires specialized (low degeneracy), highly interconnected units, and directed cycles without cross-connections do not contribute directly to experience.
An experience is identical to a conceptual structure (Φ-structure); every property of experience corresponds to a property of the Φ-structure and vice versa.
Consciousness depends on the intrinsic cause–effect power of system subsets, not on the system's interaction with its environment (functional equivalence is insufficient).

Changes in connection strengths within the neural substrate of consciousness predict changes in experience even without changes in neural activity, and similarities in Φ-structures predict similarities in experience.

The physical substrate of consciousness is localized to a complex of neuronal groups distributed over the posterior cortex and portions of the anterior cortex—not the cerebellum, basal ganglia, or peripheral pathways.

Φmax (maximally irreducible integrated information) is the quantity that identifies and measures the physical substrate of consciousness; high Φmax is the threshold criterion for a system to constitute a conscious complex.

The architecture of feedforward, largely independent processing (as in cerebellar micro-zones) cannot form a high-Φmax complex and therefore cannot constitute or be incorporated into the substrate of consciousness.
The quality or content of consciousness is identical to the form of the conceptual structure (MICS) specified by the PSC; the quantity corresponds to integrated information Φ.
Integrated information Φ measures the quantity of consciousness as the irreducibility of the conceptual structure generated by a complex.
Experience has unique borders and a particular spatio-temporal grain (exclusion postulate): the conscious system is defined by a maximal boundary excluding all other overlapping sets of elements.

n.statement: A particular experience is identical to a conceptual structure specified by a physical substrate; experience IS the conceptual structure, not merely correlated with it.
The physical substrate of consciousness must be a maximum of irreducible, intrinsic cause–effect power (Φmax); this quantity determines the quality and quantity of experience.
Digital computers running von Neumann architectures would not be conscious even when simulating human cognition, because the architecture lacks sufficient integrated cause–effect power.

The physical substrate of consciousness is a complex — the set of elements with maximal intrinsic cause–effect power (highest Φmax), assumed to be distributed over posterior cortex and portions of anterior cortex.

Consciousness requires integrated information (Φmax > 0 at a maximum); systems with feedforward, largely independent processing (e.g., cerebellar micro-zones) cannot form a high-Φmax complex and are excluded from the substrate of consciousness.

The physical substrate of consciousness and its boundaries can be empirically identified by measuring maxima of intrinsic cause–effect power at various spatial and temporal scales via perturbation and observation.
The quality/content of consciousness is identical to the form of the conceptual structure specified by the PSC; quantity corresponds to integrated information Φ.
The physical substrate of consciousness must have cause–effect power that is specific, irreducible, and maximally so (exclusion postulate); Φ gates conscious status.

The conscious system (PSC/major complex) is an architecturally delimited set of elements with high integrated cause–effect power; peripheral pathways, basal ganglia loops, and cerebellum are excluded despite influencing cortical activity.
The conceptual structure (set of concepts and their relations) is identical to the quality of experience — a strict identity, not merely a correlation.
The quantity of consciousness corresponds to maximal irreducibility Φmax — an integrated-information measure gates how much a system exists for itself.
The posterior system of consciousness (PSC) is the subset of elements with maximally irreducible cause–effect power on itself, making the locus intrinsically defined by Φmax.
Experience is necessarily integrated and irreducible to non-interdependent subsets; mere feed-forward or modular architectures without integration are excluded from consciousness.

Integrated information Φmax measures the intrinsic phenomenal capacity of the physical substrate of consciousness; Shannon information measures only extrinsic access/reporting capacity — these are distinct quantities.
Conscious information is not transmitted or broadcast from one part of the brain to another; global broadcast is denied as the mechanism of consciousness.
The physical substrate of consciousness (PSC) is located in posterior cortex, with prefrontal mechanisms serving only extrinsic reporting channels, not conscious content itself.

IIT predicts the spatio-temporal grain of the physical elements specifying consciousness is that which yields maximum integrated information (Phi), committing to a specific quantitative threshold/optimum gating conscious content.

The quantity of consciousness is measured by integrated information Φ (the minimum distance between an intact and a partitioned cause–effect structure), a non-negative number reflecting intrinsic irreducibility of the entire conceptual structure.
The PSC must be unitary and irreducible: its cause–effect structure cannot be decomposed into non-interdependent subsystems, requiring bidirectional interactions throughout.
Different experiences correspond to different conceptual structures (specific cause–effect structures), making consciousness identical to the conceptual structure specified by the PSC.

Integrated information (Φ) is information specified by a system that is irreducible to that specified by its parts, calculated as the distance between the conceptual structure of the intact system and its minimum information partition.
Any perturbation of the PSC at the appropriate spatio-temporal grain should produce a change in experience — a predicted observable commitment.

t.statement: IIT predicts that the physical substrate of consciousness (PSC) corresponds to a complex of neural elements with maximum intrinsic cause–effect power, identifying the locus of consciousness with specific neural elements rather than diffuse or prefrontal systems.

IIT predicts that changes in the efficacy of connections among elements of the primary conscious complex should lead to changes in experience even without changes in activity, and that a brain area with intact connections contributes to experience even if inactive — an empirical commitment testable by measuring connectivity rather than spiking.

c.statement: Conscious access corresponds to sudden ignition of a brain-scale network of high-level cortical areas linked by long-distance re-entrant loops.
Conscious access is measurable by late (~300 ms) global ignition of distant areas and long-distance information sharing across the workspace network.
The conscious system is a large-scale network including prefrontal, parieto-temporal, and cingulate cortices connected by long-range axons, not a posterior-only region.

Consciousness is disrupted when cortical hub function or reverberant connectivity is disrupted, particularly top-down amplification; a threshold for ignition gates the transition from subliminal to conscious processing.

Conscious access is characterized by a late, sudden 'ignition'—an all-or-none global broadcast of information across a distributed fronto-parietal network, including prefrontal and posterior parietal cortices.
Reverberant recurrent activity in the global workspace network is the mechanism that sustains conscious information over time; without it, representations cannot be broadcast and are not experienced.
Conscious access is all-or-none: a signal must be strong enough to ignite the global workspace; stimuli that fail to reach prefrontal cortex remain unconscious despite local sensory processing.
Conscious access is marked by 'ignition' of a large-scale prefronto-parietal network involving long-distance cortico-cortical synchronization.
Conscious content lives in a large-scale prefronto-parietal global neuronal workspace, not confined to posterior sensory areas.
Information becomes conscious when it is broadly broadcasted and globally accessible to many local processors across the brain.
Conscious access is characterized by a late, all-or-none (non-linear) ignition pattern rather than a graded sustained signal.

Conscious access occurs when a piece of information is selected, amplified, and broadcast via long-range axons of a core set of highly interconnected areas to all distributed cortical processors, making it globally available.
The conscious system requires a specific architecture: local specialized processors linked by a core set of highly interconnected areas with long-distance axons (fronto-parietal network).
Conscious content is sustained via long-range fronto-parietal connectivity; disruption of top-down connectivity (e.g., NMDA blockade) abolishes conscious perception.
Conscious access is marked by a late ignition event distinguishable from early feedforward activity, reflecting a phasic broadcast rather than sustained local processing.
There is a perceptual threshold in presentation time above which neurons fire and conscious recognition occurs, and below which there is little or no neural activity and no recognition.
Conscious content is reflected in late fronto-parietal activations, not early modality-specific cortical responses.
Feedforward/bottom-up processing alone is not sufficient for conscious access; recurrent top-down feedback is required.
Conscious access is marked by sudden, all-or-none ignition of prefronto-parietal networks, constituting the mechanism of conscious access.

Damage to long-distance prefrontal white matter pathways impairs conscious perception while leaving subliminal processing intact, confirming long-distance connectivity as a necessary constraint on conscious access.

The Global Neuronal Workspace is instantiated by a defined brain network of widely distributed neurons with long-range axons connecting frontal, parietal, and other cortical areas, forming the architectural locus of conscious content.
Global top-down signals related to working memory content depend on conscious processing; non-conscious modular signals persist but are not globally broadcast.

n.statement: Conscious perception involves all-or-none 'ignition' — sudden, widespread firing of stimulus-specific neurons in prefrontal and high-level cortical areas — as the mechanistic signature of global availability.

Conscious content is encoded in long-range, interconnected high-level cortical areas including lateral prefrontal cortex, anterior temporal cortex, and hippocampus — not confined to posterior sensory areas.
Consciousness (C1 global availability and C2 self-monitoring) arises specifically in the human brain, making it substrate-dependent on biological neural architecture.
Ignition and all-or-none neural firing during conscious perception are predicted observables measurable via brain-imaging and single-cell recordings.
Consciousness (C1) is the selection of information for global broadcasting, making it flexibly available across brain modules; consciousness IS this global broadcast process.
The conscious global workspace is a distributed, limited-capacity workspace in higher cortical areas that selects and holds one representation at a time for global sharing.
Conscious processing is characterised by stable, sustained representation in distributed higher cortical areas, contrasting with transient unconscious processing.
Self-monitoring (C2) is linked specifically to prefrontal and cingulate cortex circuits, distinct from the global workspace broadcast (C1).
Conscious information is globally available across the brain, enabling recall, verbal report, and action—consciousness IS global availability (C1).
Conscious access involves all-or-none selection in a capacity-limited global workspace system.
The global workspace requires long-range broadcasting architecture (prefrontal and distributed cortical regions) for conscious content.
Unconscious processing can be deep and extensive; consciousness is distinguished by global reportability, not mere processing depth.
Conscious perception operates serially and in an all-or-none manner—only one interpretation is conscious at a time—contrasting with parallel unconscious processing.
Attentional selection can operate nonconsciously; attention is necessary but not sufficient for conscious access, which requires a further distinct step.
C1 (global availability) is an elementary property present across humans, infants, and nonhuman animals, indicating it is a broadly shared architectural feature rather than a uniquely human capacity.
Consciousness requires high-level cognitive functions (C1 and C2); lower-level processing alone is insufficient.
A purely functional definition of consciousness may leave aside the experiential component ('what it is like'), raising the question of whether the theory accounts for phenomenal experience.
